domain: Strategic Studies / International Relations / Nuclear Deterrence Theory
topic_summary: Analysis of whether 'winnable great-power total war' became structurally impossible (contraction) or merely rationally avoided (dropout) after 1945. The nuclear revolution created a regime where direct superpower confrontation risked mutual annihilation, yet proxy wars, limited conflicts, and ongoing strategic debates suggest the concept may remain intellectually reachable even if politically unthinkable.

key_entities: Bernard Brodie (strategic theorist; 1946 nuclear revolution thesis)
Robert McNamara (Defense Secretary; assured destruction architect)
Kenneth Waltz (IR theorist; nuclear peace thesis)
Herman Kahn (strategic analyst; nuclear war thinkability proponent)
key_tensions: Deterrence credibility vs. use impossibility (MAD requires believable threat but use guarantees mutual destruction)
Geopolitical competition vs. direct confrontation prohibition (proxy wars as substitution mechanism)
Structural impossibility vs. rational choice constraint (contraction vs. dropout)
Post-Cold War nuclear irrelevance vs. renewed great-power competition (unipolar moment vs. multipolar return)
key_mechanisms: Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD): retaliatory capacity guarantees unacceptable damage even after first strike
Proxy war substitution: superpower competition channeled through third-party conflicts (14M deaths 1950-1989)
Assured destruction targeting: McNamara's 400-warhead countervalue doctrine
key_absences: Non-nuclear great powers (China pre-1964, major powers without arsenals) and their strategic calculus
Accidental war/unauthorized use mechanisms (technical failure modes that bypass rational deterrence)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment that nuclear weapons fundamentally altered the possibility space for great-power total war, removing 'winnable total war' from the strategic menu
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Strategic theorists, defense intellectuals, and superpower policymakers claiming interpretive authority over what nuclear weapons structurally permit

readings.commitment: Nuclear weapons created a physical impossibility: no rational path to victory exists because mutual annihilation is guaranteed
readings.authority_grounding: Mathematical game theory, MAD doctrine architects (Brodie, McNamara, Waltz)
readings.expected_structural_delta: War exits the reachable set entirely; M-set contraction (no site-expansion cell can represent this); proxy wars are substitution not continuation

readings.commitment: Nuclear weapons created a rational-choice constraint: victory remains structurally possible but costs exceed any conceivable benefit
readings.authority_grounding: Rational choice IR theory, cost-benefit deterrence models, critics of nuclear revolution thesis
readings.expected_structural_delta: War remains in reachable set but dropped from active consideration; M-set site-expansion can represent (reading still accessible); ongoing strategic debates confirm reachability

readings.commitment: Nuclear weapons created a paradox: deterrence requires credible use-threat, but use guarantees mutual destruction, so the threat is inherently incredible
readings.authority_grounding: Brennan, Kahn, limited nuclear war theorists, counterforce doctrine advocates
readings.expected_structural_delta: Deterrence is unstable; great powers seek usable nuclear options (counterforce, limited war); 'unthinkability' is rhetorical not structural; war remains reachable via escalation ladders

axiom_contradictions.basis: Contraction reading holds that no coherent strategic framework can include 'winnable nuclear war' because victory is physically impossible; dropout reading holds that victory is possible but irrational. No single framework can hold both 'victory is impossible' and 'victory is possible but too costly' as simultaneously true.

Contraction reading holds that use is impossible (guaranteed mutual annihilation removes it from possibility space); paradox reading holds that use must remain possible for deterrence to function. No framework can hold both 'use is impossible' and 'use must be credibly possible' simultaneously.
